introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah invites everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters, and to eat without paying. In the Gospel, Jesus has compassion on the crowd, and with five loaves and two fish he feeds five thousand people. Paul asks, What will separate us from the love of Christ? and answers that nothing can. Let us come to the Lord who feeds us and never stops loving us.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord opens his hand and satisfies every living thing. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may feed the hungry in body and in spirit. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the hungry of the world, and for those who work to feed them: that no one may lack daily bread. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel that nothing they have is enough: that they may bring it to Jesus and see what he can do. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are suffering, persecuted or in danger: that they may know that nothing can separate them from the love of Christ. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may receive the Eucharist with gratitude and share with those in need. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son had compassion on the crowd and fed them. Satisfy our hunger with your love, and make us generous to all who are in need. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: You give them something to eat
reflection.body:
Isaiah issues an invitation that sounds too good to be true: "Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat!" God's gifts are free. Then he asks a searching question: "Why do you spend money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which doesn't satisfy?" Many of us spend our lives on things that cannot fill us.

In the Gospel, Jesus has just heard of the death of John the Baptist and goes off to a deserted place. But the crowds follow him. Instead of sending them away, "He had compassion on them and healed their sick."

As evening comes, the disciples suggest sending the people off to buy food. Jesus answers, "They don't need to go away. You give them something to eat." The disciples have only five loaves and two fish. Jesus says, "Bring them here to me." He has the people sit on the grass, then "he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples; and the disciples gave to the multitudes." Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered.

The words took, blessed, broke and gave point to the Eucharist. And the disciples' small gift, placed in Jesus' hands, becomes more than enough. That is still how he works.

Paul asks a question that every Christian facing trouble can ask: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine?" His answer is one of the most confident statements in Scripture: nothing "will be able to separate us from God's love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."

This week, bring Jesus your five loaves: whatever little you have to offer. And give someone something to eat.
